topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A native handle is often a small integer or opaque value, but it represents an external resource with ownership and failure rules. Copying the number does not necessarily create another owned resource. This chapter wraps a Linux file descriptor in a move-only RAII type, verifies cleanup after an exception, and distinguishes destructor cleanup from an explicit checked close when an application needs to observe release errors.

blocks.text: A server closes a connection, stores the old descriptor number in a work item, and later closes that number again during cleanup. By then the operating system has reused it for another connection. The second close is not harmless tidying; it releases somebody else’s resource. The integer survived, but the ownership relationship did not.

blocks.text: This chapter turns native handles into explicit lifetime contracts. The wrapper is small, yet its design addresses copying, transfer, error reporting, exception paths, and platform-specific release behavior. Resource safety is not achieved by adding a destructor alone. It requires knowing which object is responsible for which handle at every point where control can leave the function.

topics.summary: A POSIX-style file descriptor is a process-local integer referring to an open resource. Zero is a valid descriptor, so negative one is a useful empty sentinel for an owning wrapper. blocks.text: Copying the integer creates another observer of the same descriptor number, not another independent owner. Closing through either copied number releases that descriptor, and the operating system can reuse the number for a later resource. Use dup or another appropriate API when a separate descriptor is intended, and define ownership of every returned handle immediately.

blocks.text: A file descriptor is a nonnegative integer in a process’s descriptor table. Zero is a valid descriptor, so a check such as fd > 0 is wrong for general acquisition. Native APIs commonly use a negative result to report failure. Store the successful result in an owner promptly, and keep the failure sentinel distinct from every valid descriptor value.

blocks.text: A borrowed descriptor returned by get() is not a new ownership share. It permits an operation while the owning wrapper remains alive and while no competing action invalidates the handle. A callee receiving a borrowed integer must not close it unless ownership transfer is explicitly part of the interface. Conversely, an adopting constructor assumes that the caller is handing over release responsibility rather than merely lending an integer.

blocks.text: Descriptor reuse makes stale references particularly deceptive. A pointer to freed memory may fail dramatically; a stale descriptor can successfully operate on a new resource with the same number. Therefore, “the system call succeeded” does not prove that the intended resource was used. Ownership and synchronization must prevent the stale operation in the first place.

blocks.text: Inheritance across process creation is another resource boundary. Close-on-exec flags prevent unintended descriptors from surviving a successful program-image replacement. On Linux, acquisition flags such as O_CLOEXEC avoid the race involved in creating a descriptor and setting the flag later in a multithreaded process. The flag is not a substitute for deciding which descriptors the child actually needs; process-launch code still needs an explicit inheritance plan.

topics.title: 9.1.2 Managing Socket Handles
topics.summary: On POSIX systems, sockets also use file descriptors, while other platforms expose different handle types and cleanup functions. A wrapper must match its platform’s invalid sentinel and release operation. A Windows socket cannot be treated as an ordinary POSIX descriptor simply because both are represented by small values in some builds.

blocks.text: Socket lifetime includes protocol concerns beyond closing a handle: pending output, half-close behavior, timeouts, and peer expectations may matter. RAII provides eventual resource cleanup, but a graceful application shutdown may need an explicit sequence before destruction. The network chapters build that protocol layer separately.

blocks.text: Sockets use descriptors on the Linux baseline, but their behavior is not identical to regular files. A stream socket has connection state, peer behavior, buffering, and directional shutdown. Releasing the local descriptor and announcing that no more bytes will be sent are different operations. shutdown changes communication directions; close releases the descriptor reference. A design should choose the operation that matches its protocol state. (SHUTDOWN, SOCKETS)

blocks.text: One clear ownership pattern gives each accepted connection to one worker. The listener creates the connection, moves its owner into a queue, and relinquishes responsibility. The worker owns the descriptor through receive, processing, response, and cleanup. Other components may observe metrics, but they do not independently close the same descriptor number. This pattern appears in the capstone because it simplifies both failure handling and shutdown reasoning.

blocks.text: Sharing a descriptor among threads requires a stronger protocol. A thread blocked in I/O may still be using the underlying open description while another closes its descriptor-table entry. Linux behavior does not provide a general guarantee that such a close immediately interrupts the blocked operation. Reuse of the number adds further hazards. Prefer explicit cancellation, bounded waits, and ownership coordination over closing a borrowed handle from an unrelated thread. (POSIXCLOSE)

blocks.text: Socket errors also belong to the transport layer. A peer can disconnect after a request is received but before a response is sent. Cleanup must still release the local resource, while the application records that response delivery was not confirmed. RAII prevents a leaked descriptor; it does not make the remote operation transactional or prove that the peer consumed the response.

blocks.text: Treat platform differences explicitly. Windows socket handles and release functions are not interchangeable with POSIX integer descriptors and close. A cross-platform application should provide native adapters with their own invalid-handle values, cleanup operations, and error translations. The common application layer can then depend on a stable ownership interface without pretending the underlying operating systems expose identical handle semantics.

topics.title: 9.2.1 Creating Ownership Wrappers
topics.summary: A move-only wrapper owns one valid descriptor or an empty state. Its destructor releases a valid descriptor without throwing. Move construction transfers the integer and empties the source; move assignment first releases the destination’s current resource, then transfers ownership. A get function exposes a borrowed handle for a call, while release explicitly gives ownership back to the caller.

blocks.text: A unique handle wrapper needs a small state machine: empty, owning, and transferred. Copying is disabled because copying the integer would create two apparent owners of one descriptor-table entry. Moving transfers the integer and leaves the source empty. Destruction releases only an owned handle. The operations should make it difficult to express duplicate ownership accidentally.

topics.title: 9.2.2 Guaranteeing Cleanup During Failure
topics.summary: When a scope exits through an exception, completed local owners are destroyed. This allows a function to acquire several resources sequentially without manually closing every earlier acquisition in every error branch. A constructor that fails must still arrange cleanup for any raw resource acquired before ownership was established.

Follow the target platform’s documented policy rather than a generic retry-every-EINTR rule.
